phases.title: Company revenue authority
phases.text: Bengal Diwani brings Company revenue authority in Goalpara and Sylhet. Revenue rights, military occupation and later district transfers are different changes.

phases.title: Matak becomes autonomous
phases.text: The 1805 settlement recognises Matak government under the Barsenapati within the Ahom political arrangement. The river-bounded country is shown separately from the Ahom realm.

phases.title: Burmese interventions begin
phases.text: The 1817 and 1819 interventions precede the wider occupation from 1821. They do not begin a new British annexation.

phases.title: Matak retains its own government
phases.text: Matak’s chief protects the territory during the Burmese occupation elsewhere. Matak remains separately coloured from the occupied valley.

phases.title: British advance into Assam
phases.text: British forces occupy Lower Assam in 1824 and reach Rangpur in 1825. Campaign geography remains approximate; Matak’s local government is separate.

phases.title: Yandabo; a separate Matak agreement
phases.text: Ava renounces claims and interference regarding Assam at Yandabo on 24 February. A separate May 1826 engagement leaves the Barsenapati in local government with obligations to the Company.

phases.title: Purandar restored; Matak excluded
phases.text: Purandar Singha receives a protected Upper Assam kingdom paying tribute. Matak and Sadiya remain excluded: this is not a reunion of Matak with his restored kingdom. North and south bank limits are approximate.

phases.title: Matak’s tribute agreement changes
phases.text: A January 1835 agreement substitutes tribute and a contingent obligation for the earlier arrangement. The Barsenapati continues local rule; no transfer to Purandar takes place.

phases.title: Purandar’s territory becomes directly British
phases.text: Purandar is removed in 1838. The map shows the position after that year’s annexation: his restored territory becomes British, while Matak remains separately governed.

phases.title: Matak passes to direct Company management
phases.text: After the Barsenapati’s death and rejection of revised terms by his successors, the Company assumes direct management. Sadiya’s rising and British intervention are a separate episode in the same year. This is incorporation under British rule, not Ahom reunion.

phases.title: Formal incorporation of Matak and Sadiya
phases.text: An 1842 proclamation formally incorporates both tracts into British territory and Lakhimpur district. The map remains British: the change is formal status after direct management began.

phases.title: Cachar plains and hill authority
phases.text: The Dimasa kingdom’s plains and hill territories precede separate Company arrangements. The existing hill–Barak outline is a modern-district approximation.

phases.title: Cachar plains annexed
phases.text: The Cachar plains are annexed in 1832. Tularam’s hill territory remains separate, so the hills should not turn British with the plains.

phases.title: Tularam’s territorial agreement
phases.text: The October agreement reduces/redefines the retained hill territory. Its precise dividing line is not securely reconstructed here; the map preserves a qualified hill-region proxy instead of inventing a new border.

phases.title: Remaining hill territory annexed
phases.text: The remaining Tularam hill territory passes into direct British administration. The separate Dimasa hill layer ends.

phases.title: Separate Khasi, Jaintia and Garo histories
phases.text: These regions do not form a single precolonial Meghalaya state. Local Khasi states remain distinct; the adopted Jaintia hill-region layer is retained.

phases.title: Anglo-Khasi war
phases.text: The 1829–1833 war and agreements concern local states and British routes/stations. They are not one annexation of all present Meghalaya.

phases.title: Khasi states and British relations
phases.text: Local states and British station lands have different status. The dotted Khasi-region shape locates the states without turning the whole region into a directly administered British district.

phases.title: Jaintia annexed
phases.text: Jaintia becomes British. The map retains the project’s adopted eastern-Meghalaya hills-only display; it does not reconstruct the kingdom’s Jaintiapur plains.

phases.title: Garo Hills district formed
phases.text: A district is formed with headquarters at Tura. Some interior areas remain outside effective administration; dotted regional context distinguishes this from the later extension of control.

phases.title: Garo Hills campaign
phases.text: The 1872–1873 campaign extends administration into the interior. The map switches from district context to the approximate administered region in 1873.

phases.title: Garo Hills brought under administration
phases.text: The regional Garo layer becomes British after the campaign. Modern district contours are an approximation of the region, not the surveyed 1873 boundary.

phases.title: Meghalaya autonomous within Assam
phases.text: An autonomous state is created inside Assam. The context overlay preserves the underlying Assam relationship; the modern outline does not reproduce the period’s Shillong exceptions.

phases.title: Meghalaya becomes a state
phases.text: Meghalaya gains full statehood. Its separate solid layer replaces the autonomous-within-Assam context.

phases.title: Naga communities before district administration
phases.text: No unified modern Nagaland state is projected backwards. British campaigns, district government and later frontier areas are different stages.

phases.title: Naga Hills district formed
phases.text: The district begins around the Angami/Doyang region with headquarters at Samaguting. Dotted modern-district proxies locate that stage; all present Nagaland is not annexed on this date.

phases.title: Lotha country added
phases.text: The district expands into Lotha country; Wokha becomes an administrative post. The regional context layer enlarges west/north of the earlier stage.

phases.title: Ao country added
phases.text: A further extension brings Ao country into the district. The Mokokchung-region proxy appears; trans-frontier areas are not assigned automatically.

phases.title: Naga Hills–Tuensang Area
phases.text: The Naga Hills district and Tuensang frontier area form a separate administrative unit. It is not yet the state of Nagaland.

phases.title: Nagaland becomes a state
phases.text: Statehood changes status even where the displayed regional outline stays the same.

phases.title: Lushai chiefdoms
phases.text: Local chiefs govern their communities; there is no single precolonial state matching today’s Mizoram. Campaigns do not by themselves establish a surveyed provincial boundary.

phases.title: Lushai expedition
phases.text: The 1871–1872 expedition is an earlier military intervention, distinct from permanent posts, formal annexation and the 1898 district merger.

phases.title: Posts and occupation stages
phases.text: The Lunglei post is established in 1889; northern operations and posts follow in the 1889–1890 sequence. Dotted context locates the region without asserting complete control of every village.

phases.title: Separate northern and southern administrations
phases.text: South Lushai Hills is administered from Chittagong; the north is connected to Assam. Aizawl and Lunglei markers distinguish the two centres without inventing their dividing line.

phases.title: Lushai Hills formally incorporated
phases.text: The proclamation of 6 September 1895 formally incorporates the hills. The approximate regional layer becomes solid British colour; this precedes the merger under Assam.

phases.title: Unified Lushai district joins Assam
phases.text: The northern and southern administrations merge as one Lushai Hills district under Assam. This is an administrative unification, not the first British expedition.

phases.title: Mizoram becomes a Union Territory
phases.text: Mizoram leaves Assam as a Union Territory. Its separate statehood event comes later.

phases.title: Mizoram becomes a state
phases.text: Full statehood follows the 1986 settlement.

phases.title: Manipur kingdom
phases.text: A separate kingdom; the displayed modern outline is a regional proxy and does not include all historical claims.

phases.title: Burmese occupation
phases.text: Occupation and displacement begin in 1819. The annual map uses the 1825 recovery as the next territorial stage.

phases.title: Gambhir Singh recovers Manipur
phases.text: Recovery with British support is followed by the recognition provision at Yandabo. The map returns to Manipur’s own colour.

phases.title: Restored Manipur under British protection
phases.text: Yandabo provides for Ava’s recognition of Gambhir Singh. The restored kingdom has British protection and political relations, shown with British-coloured hatching. This is different from direct British administration; the postwar 1891 settlement is a later stage.

phases.title: Kabaw boundary and compensation agreements
phases.text: Separate agreements concern the Kabaw/Kubo Valley. The source collection is linked; no unsupported precise Kabaw polygon or popular “gift” narrative is added.

phases.title: Manipur comes under British paramountcy
phases.text: British forces take over in April 1891 and impose the subsequent princely settlement. Hatching now visibly marks British paramountcy while retaining Manipur’s identity. Political oversight through Assam’s Chief Commissioner does not make Manipur an ordinary Assam district.

phases.title: Manipur accedes to the Dominion of India
phases.text: The Instrument of Accession establishes the relationship with India on specified subjects, including defence, external affairs and communications. Internal government continues before the 1949 merger. Orange hatching distinguishes accession from both British paramountcy and later central administration.

phases.title: Manipur transfers administration to India
phases.text: The merger agreement is signed on 21 September and transfers administration to the Dominion of India on 15 October 1949. The map becomes solid Indian colour. This is separate from Assam and precedes Part C constitutional status in 1950.

phases.title: Manipur becomes a Union Territory
phases.text: Constitutional status changes while the regional outline is retained.

phases.title: Manipur becomes a state
phases.text: Manipur gains statehood separately from the Assam territories reorganised by the same Act.

phases.title: Tripura before the protectorate stage
phases.text: The early-19th-century kingdom is shown in its own colour. The next phase uses NCERT’s 1809 protectorate date; earlier intervention in the region does not establish direct administration of all modern Tripura.

phases.title: Tripura accedes to the Dominion of India
phases.text: The Regent signs the Instrument of Accession on 13 August 1947. Orange hatching shows the relationship with India while internal regency administration continues. The merger and transfer of administration follow in 1949.

phases.title: Tripura transfers administration to India
phases.text: The merger agreement is signed on 9 September and transfers administration on 15 October 1949. Solid Indian colour marks central administration. Tripura does not become part of Assam; Part C status follows in 1950.

phases.title: Tripura becomes a Union Territory
phases.text: A constitutional status change, distinct from the earlier princely relationship.

phases.title: Tripura becomes a state
phases.text: Tripura gains full statehood. Its history remains separate from carving territories out of Assam.

phases.title: Frontier communities and local authorities
phases.text: The modern Arunachal outline is not projected backwards as a single historical state. Posts, political relations and effective administration expand unevenly.

phases.title: Frontier tracts and boundary context
phases.text: The 1914 frontier-tract/boundary episode appears as a dotted regional overlay. It does not imply that every part of modern Arunachal was annexed and effectively administered at once.

phases.title: Indian frontier administration
phases.text: Central responsibility and administration through the Governor of Assam are distinct from ordinary Assam state government.

phases.title: North-East Frontier Agency
phases.text: The frontier administrative reorganisation is shown as a status event without inventing a new international boundary.

phases.title: Arunachal Pradesh becomes a Union Territory
phases.text: The new Union Territory replaces the NEFA arrangement.

phases.title: Arunachal Pradesh becomes a state
phases.text: Full statehood follows on 20 February 1987.

phases.title: Postwar Assam: different local arrangements
phases.text: Company administration follows the war, but Matak and Sadiya retain separate local arrangements; Purandar’s restoration follows in 1833.

phases.title: Assam Chief Commissionership
phases.text: The new administration includes Brahmaputra/Surma valley districts and hill districts. Separate regional layers preserve the different hill and princely relationships.

phases.title: Eastern Bengal and Assam
phases.text: The new province combines Assam with Dacca, Chittagong, Rajshahi except Darjeeling, and Malda. The map uses qualified modern district groups rather than today’s entire Bangladesh.

phases.title: Separate Assam administration restored
phases.text: Assam returns to a separate Chief Commissioner’s administration. This changes provincial organisation rather than conquest.

phases.title: Independence and Sylhet partition
phases.text: Most of historical Sylhet passes to Pakistan, with retained territory in India. Today’s Sylhet division is only a regional proxy here; the detailed award line has not been reconstructed.

phases.title: Assam becomes a state
phases.text: The Constitution changes Assam’s status. Neighbouring former princely states and frontier administration remain separate sequences.

phases.title: Naga Hills–Tuensang Area separated
phases.text: The separate administrative unit precedes Nagaland’s statehood.

phases.title: Nagaland statehood
phases.text: Nagaland becomes a state; the event remains a timeline stop even without a new outline.

phases.title: Meghalaya autonomy within Assam
phases.text: The autonomous state precedes full statehood by almost two years.

phases.title: Northeast reorganisation
phases.text: Meghalaya becomes a state; Mizoram and Arunachal become Union Territories. Manipur and Tripura gain statehood through their own prior constitutional sequences.

phases.title: Mizoram and Arunachal statehood
phases.text: Both Union Territories become states on 20 February 1987. Status changes remain navigable even when their map outlines do not change.

phases.title: Tripura becomes a British protectorate
phases.text: NCERT dates protectorate status to 1809. The British-coloured hatch shows this relationship while local Manikya government continues. This is not a direct annexation of Hill Tippera into an Assam district.

phases.title: British Political Agent in Tripura
phases.text: Appointment of a resident Political Agent makes British oversight more explicit. Tripura is displayed as a princely state under British paramountcy, with the British hatch and its own local outline.

phases.title: Manipur becomes an Indian Part C state
phases.text: The Constitution places Manipur among the Part C states from 26 January 1950. This follows the October 1949 transfer of administration and precedes Union Territory status in 1956.

phases.title: Tripura becomes an Indian Part C state
phases.text: The Constitution places Tripura among the Part C states from 26 January 1950. This follows the October 1949 transfer of administration and precedes Union Territory status in 1956.
